full_judgment:
7. Ms Sara Hossain, learned Senior Advocate at the outset submits that the continued mandatory requirement in electronic forms for including both the father and mother's names to register for JS, SSC and HS C examinations is in total violation of the fundamental rights to equality before law guaranteed under Article 27, in that it means that children who are not acknowledged by their fathers, or who do not know who their fathers are and cannot provide their information on any public records are deprived of the opportunity to be admitted for public examinations, unlike other children who can do so. This continued mandatory requirement in the electronic forms of including both the father and the mother's names to register for any examination that is the JSC, SSC and HS C is arbitrary inasmuch as there is no rational basis for requiring such in formation. She further brought to the notice of the Court that the National Policy on Women's Development 1997 for the first time provided that the mother's name was to be included on all government forms and documents in addition to the father's name. This policy measure was adopted in order to ensure furtherance of the Government's commitment to ensure gender equality. The policy, as one of the objectives to be achieved, included the adoption of "measures to identify a child on the basis of the identity of the parents; i.e. to use the name of both father and mother in birth registration, in all certificates, in voters list, in forms and in applications for employment, passport etc." Whilst this sought to further equality, in particular gender equality, by according equal recognition to both the father and the mother of a child, it has in practice led to a denial of equality and to discrimination against the individuals who cannot provide the identity of their fathers.
